candidates.rule: Do not include implementation details in the whatsnew entries.
candidates.why: The maintainers want whatsnew entries to focus only on user-facing changes, not internal implementation details.

candidates.rule: Place whatsnew entries in the appropriate section based on the feature area.
candidates.why: Maintainers expect entries to be organized by topic, such as moving I/O-related changes to the I/O section.

candidates.rule: Do not add whatsnew entries for tests, documentation edits, or error message changes.
candidates.why: These changes are not considered user-facing and do not require release notes.

candidates.rule: Use ASCII characters instead of Unicode symbols in whatsnew entries.
candidates.why: The project prefers to keep text compatible and readable without special characters.

candidates.rule: Avoid creating new sections in whatsnew unless necessary; use existing sections like 'Other' when appropriate.
candidates.why: Maintainers prefer to keep the structure simple and avoid unnecessary sections.

candidates.rule: Combine duplicate or nearly identical whatsnew entries into a single entry.
candidates.why: This reduces redundancy and keeps the changelog clean and concise.

candidates.rule: Reference the correct PR or issue number when documenting fixes.
candidates.why: Accuracy in referencing ensures proper attribution and traceability.

candidates.rule: Only document public API changes in whatsnew entries.
candidates.why: Private or non-public methods should not be included in release notes.

candidates.rule: Ensure accuracy when describing behavior changes and provide examples if needed.
candidates.why: Inaccurate descriptions can mislead users about what has changed.

candidates.rule: Include both Series and DataFrame equivalents when documenting method changes.
candidates.why: Users expect consistent documentation across similar APIs.

candidates.rule: Use consistent method naming with :meth: and :class: directives in whatsnew entries.
candidates.why: This ensures proper formatting and linking in the generated documentation.

candidates.rule: Write whatsnew entries concisely, focusing only on user-facing impact and avoiding internal details or error messages.
candidates.why: The maintainers want changelog entries to be actionable and understandable for users, not cluttered with implementation specifics.

candidates.rule: Only include bugfixes in whatsnew if they are significant and user-facing; minor or internal fixes do not require an entry.
candidates.why: The maintainers aim to keep the changelog focused on meaningful changes for users.

candidates.rule: Categorize changes in the correct whatsnew section, such as moving I/O-related bugfixes from API changes to the I/O bugfixes section.
candidates.why: Proper categorization helps users quickly locate relevant changes.

candidates.rule: Mention both horizontal and vertical variants (e.g. barh) when documenting plotting functionality.
candidates.why: Users may rely on either form, so both should be documented for completeness.

candidates.rule: Move documentation of conversion-related changes to the Conversion section in whatsnew.
candidates.why: Ensures consistent organization of changelog entries by topic.

candidates.rule: Avoid default parameters in Cython function signatures.
candidates.why: Default parameters in Cython can lead to unexpected behavior or compilation issues.

candidates.rule: Ensure test coverage for edge cases such as small sample sizes when bias=False returns NAN and bias=True does not.
candidates.why: The maintainers require confidence that numerical edge cases are correctly handled.

candidates.rule: Check for both contiguity directions in performance-critical code to avoid regressions.
candidates.why: Failing to do so may cause performance issues in non-contiguous array cases.

candidates.rule: When fixing bugs involving extension dtypes, ensure the fix is general or accurately reflect its limited scope in the changelog.
candidates.why: Avoid misleading users by claiming a broader fix than was implemented.

candidates.rule: Clarify when a bugfix affects specific system configurations, such as older systems with particular tzdata toolchains.
candidates.why: Helps users understand whether they were actually affected by the bug.

candidates.rule: Use C++ types like std::string_view and std::span instead of C-style pointers and arrays in C++ files.
candidates.why: Using modern C++ types improves type safety, reduces pointer arithmetic, and leverages standard library functionality.

candidates.rule: Prefer std::pair or std::subspan over custom POD types to return data and size from functions.
candidates.why: Standard library types like std::span with subspan provide a cleaner, more idiomatic way to signal written data and size.

candidates.rule: Use C++20 ranges and views like std::ranges::views::lazy_split instead of iterator-based designs when possible.
candidates.why: Ranges provide a more modern, efficient, and readable way to process sequences in a single pass.

candidates.rule: Declare variables with auto instead of using static_cast for type conversion.
candidates.why: Using auto follows modern C++ best practices and improves readability and maintainability.

candidates.rule: Replace C-style casts with direct initialization or appropriate C++ casts.
candidates.why: C-style casts are unsafe and unnecessary in C++; direct initialization or C++ casts are preferred.

candidates.rule: Move extern "C" linkage declarations to header files and avoid repeating them in source files.
candidates.why: The extern "C" linkage is already specified in the header, so repeating it in the source is redundant.

candidates.rule: Use assertions instead of comments to enforce preconditions like tsep != '\0'.
candidates.why: Assertions ensure conditions are checked at runtime, making the code safer and more reliable.

candidates.rule: Avoid unnecessary pointer arithmetic by using modern C++ features and standard library functions.
candidates.why: Pointer arithmetic is error-prone and unidiomatic in C++; modern C++ provides safer and clearer alternatives.

candidates.rule: Remove unnecessary indirections and use function arguments directly.
candidates.why: Direct use of arguments improves clarity and reduces complexity.

candidates.rule: Rename source files to reflect their broader functionality when they no longer match the original single-purpose name.
candidates.why: A more generic name improves intuitiveness and maintainability as the file's responsibilities evolve.

candidates.rule: Move function declarations to headers when moving non-static functions between source files.
candidates.why: Corresponding header declarations must be updated to reflect function location changes.

candidates.rule: Avoid using memcpy for individual assignments; use it for bulk memory operations only.
candidates.why: Using memcpy for single assignments is less readable and unnecessary when direct assignment suffices.

candidates.rule: Place extern blocks in header files, not in source files.
candidates.why: Extern blocks belong in headers to ensure consistent linkage across translation units.

candidates.rule: Use from_chars_advanced with appropriate chars_format options instead of reusing fast_float_strtod.
candidates.why: from_chars_advanced provides more precise control over parsing options and is the intended modern interface.

candidates.rule: Include documentation about return values and side effects in header files, not in source files.
candidates.why: Header files are the interface; documentation there ensures users see it without inspecting implementation details.

candidates.rule: Keep the original text in docstrings when it accurately reflects the behavior, especially if the parameters have actual effects beyond compatibility.
candidates.why: The original text should be preserved because the parameters in question have real effects when passed to numpy functions, not just for compatibility.

candidates.rule: Combine related conditional checks into a single line and include a comment explaining the reason for the logic.
candidates.why: Combining checks improves readability and the comment helps clarify the intent, such as why sorting is skipped for Series.

candidates.rule: Minimize code changes by reverting unnecessary modifications when the resulting behavior and messages remain unchanged.
candidates.why: The project prefers to keep diffs small and avoid changes that don't alter functionality or improve clarity.

candidates.rule: Use `get_indexer_for` instead of special-casing specific index types like IntervalIndex.
candidates.why: Using `get_indexer_for` avoids the need for type-specific handling and improves code robustness.

candidates.rule: Ensure axis handling is robust by calling `_get_axis_number` early to support both integer and string axis specifications.
candidates.why: Delaying the `_get_axis_number` check can hide bugs when axis is passed as a string like 'index'.

candidates.rule: Pass `deep=False` when copying objects unless a deep copy is explicitly required.
candidates.why: Shallow copies are sufficient in many cases and more efficient; deep copies should be intentional.

candidates.rule: Update tolerance-related docstrings when making changes to tolerance behavior.
candidates.why: The tolerance docstring must reflect current behavior to avoid user confusion.

candidates.rule: Link to documentation using the dev version URL when the target page is not yet live in stable releases.
candidates.why: Linking to the dev docs ensures the link works both before and after a release, avoiding broken redirects.

candidates.rule: Modify `result` in place using `ensure_index_from_sequences` when updating index structures in merge operations.
candidates.why: In-place updates to `result.index` are necessary to maintain correct index structure within the current code design.

candidates.rule: Use single quotes for string literals in docstrings when they are more accurate or conventional.
candidates.why: Single quotes are preferred in certain contexts for consistency and accuracy in documentation.

candidates.rule: Use sets for efficient comparison of index names in Series operations.
candidates.why: Sets provide a clean and performant way to compare collections of names, such as in MultiIndex compatibility checks.

candidates.rule: Ensure deprecation warnings are actionable by suggesting an alternative approach to users.
candidates.why: Deprecation messages should guide users on what to do instead, such as manually aligning indexes.

candidates.rule: Keep behavior consistent across similar operations by applying the same deprecation policy to analogous methods.
candidates.why: Consistency in deprecation helps avoid confusion and ensures uniform behavior across the API.

candidates.rule: Avoid special-casing rare edge cases unless they are common enough to justify stricter behavior.
candidates.why: The current behavior is considered acceptable for rare cases, and stricter rules may not be necessary.

candidates.rule: Improve error messages by clarifying when duplicate level values are detected, even if not explicitly passed.
candidates.why: The message should not mislead users into thinking they passed duplicates when the issue arose internally.

candidates.rule: Add a comment referencing the GitHub issue URL on the first line of every new test.
candidates.why: To ensure each test is traceable to the issue it fixes or addresses.

candidates.rule: Parametrize tests over engine when testing evaluation or computation functionality.
candidates.why: To ensure coverage across different evaluation engines and reproduce engine-specific bugs.

candidates.rule: Use pytest fixtures for shared test data instead of defining helper methods or variables.
candidates.why: To promote reusability, clarity, and integration with pytest's fixture system.

candidates.rule: Avoid constructing DataFrame objects in tests when simpler alternatives are sufficient.
candidates.why: To reduce test complexity and focus on the minimal code needed to reproduce the behavior.

candidates.rule: Parametrize test cases instead of writing repetitive test logic for different values.
candidates.why: To improve test maintainability and clarity when testing multiple input combinations.

candidates.rule: Place imports at the top of the test file.
candidates.why: To follow Python conventions and ensure clarity about dependencies.

candidates.rule: Do not include docstrings in test functions.
candidates.why: Because tests generally do not require docstrings and the practice is not standard in the codebase.

candidates.rule: Avoid redundant or duplicative tests that do not add new coverage.
candidates.why: To maintain a clean and efficient test suite without unnecessary duplication.

candidates.rule: Use clear and accurate names for test variables to reflect their purpose.
candidates.why: To avoid confusion when reading tests, especially when logic depends on negated conditions.

candidates.rule: Follow the pattern of assigning test results to a variable named `result` before assertion.
candidates.why: To maintain consistency across tests and improve readability.

candidates.rule: Remove comments that merely repeat what the code already clearly expresses.
candidates.why: To reduce noise and keep test code clean and focused.

candidates.rule: Add a comment inside the test body explaining the motivation for the test, including the GitHub issue number and which code path it exercises.
candidates.why: This helps clarify the purpose of the test and which part of the code it is validating, especially for future maintainers.

candidates.rule: Use only the beginning of a warning message when testing for deprecation warnings, unless custom formatting is involved.
candidates.why: The beginning of the message is sufficient to identify the warning, and testing the full message is unnecessary if no custom formatting is applied.

candidates.rule: Replace references to 'object dtype' with 'EA' in test comments when the test cases involve extension array types.
candidates.why: The values are no longer of object dtype in most test builds, but the test remains valid as the code handles 'object or EA'.

candidates.rule: Start each test with a comment referencing the associated GitHub issue.
candidates.why: This provides immediate context about the issue being tested and improves traceability.

candidates.rule: Parametrize tests when testing multiple related cases to improve code reuse and clarity.
candidates.why: Parametrization avoids code duplication and makes it easier to extend test coverage.

candidates.rule: Use `tm.assert_frame_equal`, `tm.assert_series_equal`, or similar to check the full state of the object, including index, columns, and dtypes.
candidates.why: This ensures the result matches the expected output in all aspects, not just values.

candidates.rule: Use the `@td.skip_if_no` decorator to skip tests requiring optional dependencies during test collection.
candidates.why: Skipping during collection is more efficient and avoids unnecessary test execution.

candidates.rule: Avoid using one-letter variable names in tests.
candidates.why: Descriptive variable names improve readability and maintainability of test code.

candidates.rule: Avoid using `check_dtype=False` unless absolutely necessary; instead, ensure the expected and actual dtypes match.
candidates.why: This ensures that dtype correctness is validated, which is important for correctness in operations that depend on dtypes.

candidates.rule: Do not document previous behavior in test comments; focus on current behavior and motivation.
candidates.why: Documenting past behavior leads to clutter and becomes outdated; tests should reflect current expectations.

candidates.rule: Assert the full warning message or a meaningful part of it when testing for warnings.
candidates.why: This ensures the correct warning is raised with the expected content.

candidates.rule: Remove unused variables like `request` from test functions.
candidates.why: Unused variables are unnecessary and can confuse readers about the test's intent.

candidates.rule: Use hard-coded expected values instead of relying on `check_dtype=False` when comparing dictionaries.
candidates.why: Hard-coded values make the test more explicit and avoid bypassing dtype checks.

candidates.rule: Fix indentation so test functions are not nested inside other tests.
candidates.why: Nested tests are not discovered by pytest and will not be executed.

candidates.rule: Avoid using `inplace=True` in tests unless the test is specifically about inplace operations.
candidates.why: Using `inplace=True` complicates debugging and is not the default; prefer reassignment.

candidates.rule: Add comments referencing GitHub issues instead of including issue details in test names.
candidates.why: This keeps test names clean and moves explanatory details to comments where they belong.

candidates.rule: Split complex test functions into smaller, more focused tests to improve debuggability.
candidates.why: Smaller tests are easier to understand and debug when failures occur.

candidates.rule: Test with standard zoneinfo timezones instead of dateutil when the bug is not specific to dateutil.
candidates.why: Using standard timezones improves consistency and reduces dependency on external libraries.

candidates.rule: Test with both np.int32 and np.int64 when testing integer dtype behavior.
candidates.why: To ensure compatibility and correct handling of different integer types in the code.

candidates.rule: Include non-January 1 dates in tests involving date scalars.
candidates.why: To ensure tests cover a broader range of date values and avoid edge cases specific to year-start dates.

candidates.rule: Place interval index tests in tests.arrays.interval.test_interval instead of tests.indexes.interval.test_interval.
candidates.why: To maintain proper test organization and alignment with the module structure.

candidates.rule: Check the full state of the result using tm.assert_index_equal with an explicitly constructed expected index.
candidates.why: To ensure complete and accurate comparison of index objects beyond just basic equality.

candidates.rule: Avoid using inplace operations in tests unless the test is specifically about inplace behavior.
candidates.why: To ensure tests focus on the intended functionality and are easier to understand and maintain.

candidates.rule: Remove print statements from tests unless they are actively being used for debugging.
candidates.why: To keep test output clean and avoid noise during test runs.

candidates.rule: Generate test files at runtime instead of adding them to the repository.
candidates.why: To reduce repository bloat and ensure test files are created in a controlled, reproducible manner.

candidates.rule: Use the tmp_excel fixture for Excel writer tests to maintain consistency with other writer tests.
candidates.why: To standardize test setup and teardown across Excel writer test files.

candidates.rule: Link new tests to their corresponding GitHub issue or PR using a comment.
candidates.why: To provide traceability and context for why a test was added.

candidates.rule: Check the full result in format tests by comparing against an expected list or structure.
candidates.why: To make tests more robust and ensure they validate complete output rather than partial results.

candidates.rule: Write tests that actually exercise the bug being fixed, not just pass on main.
candidates.why: To ensure tests are meaningful and catch regressions.

candidates.rule: Use only the GitHub issue reference format like #GH19129 in comments, without additional text.
candidates.why: To maintain a consistent and concise style for issue references in the codebase.

candidates.rule: Test with integers that exceed numpy int bounds when testing JSON serialization of large integers.
candidates.why: To ensure correct handling of large integers that cannot be represented by numpy dtypes.

candidates.rule: Use np.ulonglong(2**64 - 1) to test maximum unsigned 64-bit integer values.
candidates.why: To validate behavior at the limits of unsigned 64-bit integer representation.

candidates.rule: Move test functions to the appropriate test class, such as TestUltraJSONTests for ujson-specific tests.
candidates.why: To maintain proper organization and grouping of related tests.

candidates.rule: Use TypeError for invalid type errors in ujson tests unless another exception type is specifically required.
candidates.why: To maintain consistency with Python's standard type error handling.

candidates.rule: Assert on the output of read_csv directly in parser tests.
candidates.why: To ensure tests validate the actual parsing result rather than intermediate values.

candidates.rule: Test with object-dtype indexes when the test requires non-numeric index types.
candidates.why: To ensure correct behavior when indexes are not backed by numeric dtypes.

candidates.rule: Add high-precision float values like pi to float parametrization in JSON table schema tests.
candidates.why: To test correct handling of many-digit floating-point numbers in serialization.

candidates.rule: Avoid using StringIO for tests that need to exercise parallel CSV parsing logic.
candidates.why: Because StringIO does not trigger the same code paths as file-like objects that support parallelization.

candidates.rule: Do not restrict tests to pyarrow_parser_only unless the behavior is engine-specific.
candidates.why: Because functionality should work consistently across all parsing engines unless otherwise specified.

candidates.rule: Place imports at the top of the test file.
candidates.why: To follow Python coding standards and make dependencies clear at a glance.

candidates.rule: Split test cases with multiple assertions into separate tests with descriptive names.
candidates.why: To improve test clarity and make it easier to identify which specific case fails.

candidates.rule: Check the dtype of MultiIndex codes when testing MultiIndex equivalence.
candidates.why: Because the MultiIndex constructor normalizes dtypes, which can mask issues in the test data.

candidates.rule: When changing behavior, add tests and a note in the whatsnew for the next minor release.
candidates.why: To ensure changes are properly documented and tested before release.

candidates.rule: Report column numbers as 1-based in validation scripts.
candidates.why: Because columns are typically reported as 1-based in tooling and error messages.
